content: Hepatitis B is a significant global health issue, as recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO). The causative agent, the hepatitis B virus (HBV), is a double-stranded DNA virus belonging to the Hepadnaviridae family. This virus primarily targets the liver, leading to both acute and chronic infections. The immune response of the host during HBV infection contributes to liver cell damage (hepatocellular damage) and viral clearance. The HBV virion attaches to specific receptors on the surface of hepatocytes and enters the cells, where it utilizes the host's cellular machinery to replicate its genome and produce viral proteins. Transmission of HBV occurs through exposure to infectious blood or bodily fluids. Chronic HBV infection is strongly associated with the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). Immune complexes, such as those formed by surface antigens and antibodies, play a critical role in the disease's pathogenesis. Hepatitis B must be distinguished from other conditions that present with similar symptoms, such as fever, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), icteric sclera (yellowing of the eyes), and elevated liver enzymes (ALT and AST). Differential diagnoses include other viral hepatitis strains, alcoholic hepatitis, and autoimmune hepatitis. The risk of HBV infection is highest in individuals with certain lifestyles, occupations, or environments that involve frequent contact with infected blood. High-risk groups include immigrants or refugees from areas with high HBV prevalence, injecting drug users, men who have sex with men (MSM), patients undergoing hemodialysis, and household contacts of HBV carriers. Perinatal transmission from an infected mother to her infant is highly efficient, with a 70–90% transmission rate if the mother is positive for both HBsAg and HBeAg, in the absence of post-exposure prophylaxis. The diagnosis of hepatitis B is based on biochemical assessment of liver function and confirmed by the detection of specific antigens and antibodies in the serum. Serologic markers such as HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HBc IgG, HBeAg, and anti-HBe are used to confirm the diagnosis and monitor the disease course. Initial laboratory findings often reveal elevated bilirubin, ALT, AST, and alkaline phosphatase levels, along with decreased protein levels. Prothrombin time may be prolonged in cases of severe liver damage. In most adult patients, the immune system can clear the virus without treatment. However, there is currently no specific treatment for acute hepatitis B infection. Antiviral therapy is rarely required, except in cases of fulminant hepatitis, which occurs in less than 1% of patients. For chronic HBV infection, treatment may be necessary to reduce the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer. Available antiviral drugs, such as lamivudine, adefovir, tenofovir, telbivudine, and entecavir, as well as immune system modulators like interferon alpha-2a and pegylated interferon-alpha-2a, can suppress viral replication and minimize liver damage. However, these treatments do not eradicate the virus. Treatment duration typically ranges from six months to a year, depending on the medication and HBV genotype. Hepatitis B vaccination is the most effective method of prevention. The vaccine, composed of the HBV surface antigen (HBsAg), is administered in a series of three doses. Vaccination of infants, particularly within 24 hours of birth, is 90–95% effective in preventing HBV infection and transmission when followed by at least two additional doses. Universal infant vaccination programs have significantly reduced the prevalence of chronic HBV infection in many regions. However, a small proportion of vaccinated individuals (5–10%) may have a poor response to the vaccine and remain susceptible to HBV infection as adults. For newborns of HBsAg-positive mothers, a combination of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and the HBV vaccine is administered shortly after birth to provide passive and active immunity. This approach significantly reduces the risk of vertical transmission. Without post-exposure immunoprophylaxis, approximately 40% of infants born to HBV-infected mothers in the United States will develop chronic HBV infection, with one-fourth of these individuals eventually succumbing to chronic liver disease. In cases of advanced liver damage or liver failure due to HBV infection, liver transplantation may be considered. Routine screening for HBV infection is recommended for high-risk groups, including immigrants from endemic areas, individuals with chronically elevated liver enzymes, immunocompromised patients, and those with a history of injection drug use. Additionally, HBV carriers over 40 years of age with persistent ALT elevation or high HBV DNA levels should be screened for hepatocellular carcinoma. The natural history of hepatitis B is highly variable, with clinical manifestations depending on the age at infection, immune status, and stage of disease recognition. Acute hepatitis B has an incubation period of 45 to 120 days, during which patients may experience flu-like symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and headaches. While most individuals recover completely, some may become asymptomatic carriers, develop chronic disease, or progress to fulminant hepatitis. Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or hepatocellular carcinoma. The prognosis for acute hepatitis B is generally favorable, with symptoms resolving within 2–3 weeks. However, infants and immunocompromised individuals are at higher risk of developing chronic disease.
